text: What is a Geographical Indication (GI)? A Geographical Indication is a sign used on goods that have a specific geographical origin and possess qualities, reputation or characteristics essentially attributable to that place of origin. Examples include Darjeeling tea, Champagne, and Banarasi sarees. A GI links a product to a territory and to the traditional methods and natural conditions of that region, and it is a collective right belonging to producers of that region rather than to a single owner. In India, GIs are protected under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999, which came into force in 2003, in compliance with the WTO TRIPS Agreement. GIs cover agricultural, natural, manufactured and handicraft goods, and foodstuffs. Registration prevents unauthorised parties from using the indication on goods not originating from the region or not meeting the required standards, thereby protecting both producers and consumers.

How is a Geographical Indication registered in India? Registration is handled by the Geographical Indications Registry (part of the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks) in Chennai, under the GI Act 1999. Steps: (1) An association of producers, organisation or authority representing the interest of the producers (not an individual, generally) files an application in the prescribed form with a Statement of Case describing the goods, the geographical area, the quality/characteristics linked to origin, the method of production, and a map. (2) The application is examined; an Examination Report and a Consultative Group review may follow. (3) If accepted, the GI is advertised in the GI Journal for opposition. (4) Any person may oppose within the prescribed period (typically three months, extendable). (5) If unopposed or the opposition fails, the GI is registered. Registration is initially for 10 years and is renewable indefinitely in 10-year terms. Separately, producers can apply to be registered as 'authorised users' to actually use the GI.

What are some famous registered Geographical Indications of India? India's first registered GI was Darjeeling tea (2004). Other well-known Indian GIs include: Banarasi sarees and brocades (Uttar Pradesh); Kanchipuram silk (Tamil Nadu); Mysore silk and Mysore sandalwood (Karnataka); Pochampally Ikat (Telangana); Kolhapuri chappals (Maharashtra/Karnataka); Nagpur oranges; Alphonso mango (Maharashtra); Basmati rice; Tirupati laddu; Bikaneri bhujia; Madhubani paintings (Bihar); Channapatna toys (Karnataka); Kashmir Pashmina and Kashmir saffron; Naga Mircha (Naga king chilli); Feni (Goa); and Chanderi and Maheshwari fabrics (Madhya Pradesh). These span agricultural produce, textiles, handicrafts and foodstuffs, and each represents a product whose reputation and qualities are tied to a specific Indian region and traditional know-how.

What are the benefits of registering a Geographical Indication? (1) Legal protection - registration gives producers of the region the exclusive right to use the indication and to prevent others from using it on goods not originating there or not meeting the standards, and unauthorised use is an infringement. (2) Prevention of misappropriation and passing off - it guards traditional and regional products against imitation and biopiracy (as sought for Basmati). (3) Premium value and market access - a GI signals authenticity and quality, allowing producers to command higher prices and access export markets. (4) Collective economic benefit - because a GI is a community right, its gains flow to all genuine producers of the region, supporting rural livelihoods and traditional artisans. (5) Consumer protection - buyers can trust the origin and quality. (6) Cultural preservation - it recognises and sustains traditional skills, knowledge and heritage tied to a locality. A GI does not, however, protect the technology or recipe from being independently used elsewhere under a different name.

How is a Geographical Indication enforced? Once registered, a GI can be enforced against infringers and those passing off goods. Under the GI Act 1999: registered proprietors and authorised users can bring civil suits for infringement seeking injunctions, damages or an account of profits, and delivery-up of infringing goods. The Act also creates criminal offences - falsely applying a GI, selling goods with a false GI, or falsifying entries - punishable with imprisonment (generally six months to three years) and fines. Infringement includes using the indication in a way that misleads about origin, that constitutes unfair competition, or that uses a GI for goods not originating in the indicated region even with words like 'kind', 'style', 'imitation'. Customs measures can help stop infringing imports/exports. For international protection, producers must register or seek protection in other countries separately (e.g. through those countries' GI or certification-mark systems), since Indian registration is territorial.

section: Who Can Apply for a GI
text: Who can apply for a Geographical Indication and who can use it? A GI application must be made by an association of persons, producers, organisation or authority established by or under law that represents the interest of the producers of the goods concerned - not by a single individual for private benefit, because a GI is a collective right. The applicant becomes the 'registered proprietor' holding the GI for the benefit of all eligible producers. Individual producers who make the goods in the defined region according to the specified standards can then apply separately to be entered on the register as 'authorised users', which gives them the right to actually use the GI on their goods and to sue for infringement. This two-tier structure (proprietor plus authorised users) ensures the indication remains a shared regional asset while still allowing genuine producers to benefit and enforce it.

What is the difference between a Geographical Indication and a Trademark? A trademark is a sign that distinguishes the goods or services of one enterprise from those of others; it is owned by a single business, can be licensed or assigned, and identifies commercial source. A Geographical Indication identifies goods as originating from a particular place and having qualities or reputation due to that origin; it is a collective right of all qualifying producers of the region, cannot be owned or monopolised by one trader, and cannot be assigned or licensed to outsiders. A trademark can, in principle, be used anywhere by its owner, whereas a GI can only be used by producers in the designated region meeting the standards. Both are registrable IP rights in India (Trade Marks Act 1999 and GI Act 1999 respectively). A regional product can benefit from both - a GI for the origin-linked authenticity and individual producers' trademarks for their own brands within that GI.

How does the TRIPS Agreement treat Geographical Indications? The WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) requires all member countries to provide legal means for interested parties to protect Geographical Indications (Articles 22-24). Article 22 gives a general standard of protection against use that misleads the public as to origin or amounts to unfair competition. Article 23 gives a higher, additional level of protection specifically for wines and spirits, prohibiting use of a GI on such products not originating in the place even where the true origin is indicated or the term is accompanied by 'kind', 'type', 'style' or 'imitation'. Article 24 contains exceptions and provides for negotiations to increase protection. India enacted the GI Act 1999 to comply with these TRIPS obligations. Developing countries, including India, have pressed for extending the higher Article 23 level of protection beyond wines and spirits to other products such as Basmati rice and Darjeeling tea.

section: GI Documentation and Statement of Case
text: What documentation is needed to register a GI in India? A GI application must be accompanied by a Statement of Case that establishes the link between the product and its geographical origin. It typically includes: the class and description of the goods; the geographical area of production with a clear map; the specific quality, reputation or characteristics of the goods and how they are essentially attributable to the region (climate, soil, raw materials, traditional human skill); the method and standards of production/processing that authorised users must follow; historical evidence and the reputation of the product; details of the applicant association and how it represents the producers; and an inspection/verification mechanism to ensure goods bearing the GI meet the standards. Strong applications document tradition, uniqueness and the origin-quality link thoroughly, since this evidence is central to both examination and defending the GI against opposition or infringement.

How long does a Geographical Indication last and how is it renewed? A registered Geographical Indication in India is protected for an initial period of 10 years from the date of registration. It can be renewed indefinitely for successive periods of 10 years each on payment of the prescribed renewal fee before expiry (with provisions for restoration within a limited period if renewal is missed). This means a GI, unlike a patent, can potentially last forever so long as it is renewed and the product continues to meet its standards - reflecting that the origin-quality link and traditional reputation endure over time. Authorised-user registrations are tied to the GI and also require maintenance. Because protection is perpetual if renewed, GIs are a durable tool for safeguarding traditional regional products, in contrast to the fixed 20-year term of patents.
